science.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
science.expl: Au comes from the Latin 'aurum' meaning gold. Silver is Ag (argentum), Iron is Fe (ferrum), Copper is Cu (cuprum).

science.q: What planet is known as the Red Planet?
science.expl: Mars appears red due to iron oxide (rust) on its surface. It has the largest volcano in the solar system — Olympus Mons.

science.q: What is the powerhouse of the cell?
science.expl: Mitochondria generate most of the cell's ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the energy currency. They have their own DNA.

science.q: What particle has a negative charge?
science.expl: Electrons carry a negative charge (-1). Protons are positive (+1), neutrons are neutral, and photons carry no charge.

science.q: What is the hardest natural substance on Earth?
science.expl: Diamond rates 10 on the Mohs hardness scale. Its carbon atoms form a rigid tetrahedral structure making it extremely hard.

science.q: What is the speed of light approximately?
science.expl: Light travels at approximately 299,792 km/s in a vacuum. This is the universal speed limit according to Einstein's relativity.

science.q: What is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere?
science.expl: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere. Oxygen is about 21%, and argon roughly 0.93%.
Rainbows form when sunlight is refracted, dispersed, and reflected inside water droplets, splitting white light into its component colors.

science.q: What is the atomic number of Carbon?
science.expl: Carbon has 6 protons, giving it atomic number 6. It forms 4 covalent bonds, making it the backbone of organic chemistry.
The pancreas contains beta cells in the Islets of Langerhans that produce insulin to regulate blood sugar.

science.q: What type of bond involves sharing electrons?
science.expl: In covalent bonds, atoms share electron pairs. Ionic bonds involve electron transfer. Most bonds have some character of both.

science.q: How many chromosomes do humans have?
science.expl: Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). The 23rd pair determines biological sex. Chimpanzees have 48.

science.q: What is the second law of thermodynamics about?
science.expl: The second law states that entropy (disorder) of an isolated system always increases. Heat flows naturally from hot to cold.

science.q: What is the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle?
opts: You can't know both position and momentum exactly
science.expl: Heisenberg showed that precisely knowing a particle's position limits knowledge of its momentum, and vice versa — fundamental to quantum mechanics.
Dark matter doesn't interact with electromagnetic radiation but its existence is inferred from gravitational effects on visible matter. It makes up ~27% of the universe.

history.q: In which year did World War II end?
history.expl: WWII ended in 1945 — Germany surrendered in May (V-E Day) and Japan in August (V-J Day) after the atomic bombings.

history.q: The ancient city of Machu Picchu is in which country?
history.expl: Machu Picchu was built by the Inca Empire in the 15th century, sitting at 2,430m in the Andes Mountains of Peru.

history.q: Which civilization built the pyramids of Giza?
history.expl: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Khufu. It was the tallest man-made structure for over 3,800 years.
The Silk Road was a network of trade routes connecting East Asia to the Mediterranean, facilitating exchange of goods and ideas for over 1,500 years.

history.q: Which empire was ruled by Genghis Khan?
history.expl: Genghis Khan founded the Mongol Empire in 1206 — the largest contiguous land empire in history.

history.q: Who was the first Emperor of Rome?
history.expl: Augustus (born Octavian) became the first Roman Emperor in 27 BC. Julius Caesar was dictator but never emperor.

history.q: What year did the Berlin Wall fall?
history.expl: The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, symbolizing the end of the Cold War. Germany reunified in 1990.

history.q: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
history.expl: Thomas Jefferson was the principal author, with edits by Franklin and Adams. It was adopted on July 4, 1776.
The Renaissance (14th-17th century) was a cultural movement originating in Italy, marked by renewed interest in classical learning.

history.q: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic?
history.expl: Amelia Earhart accomplished this in 1932. She later disappeared over the Pacific in 1937.
Signed in 1215 by King John, the Magna Carta limited royal authority and established that everyone, including the king, was subject to law.

opts: Geopolitical tension between US and USSR
history.expl: The Cold War (1947-1991) was geopolitical tension between NATO and Warsaw Pact without direct military conflict between the superpowers.

history.q: What caused the Black Death in medieval Europe?
history.expl: The Black Death (1347-1351) was caused by Yersinia pestis, transmitted by fleas on rats. It killed 30-60% of Europe's population.

history.q: Which country was first to grant women the right to vote nationally?
history.expl: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant all women the right to vote in national elections in 1893.

history.q: In what year did the Battle of Thermopylae take place?
history.expl: Fought in 480 BC, this battle saw King Leonidas and 300 Spartans (along with other Greeks) delay the massive Persian army of Xerxes I.

geography.q: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
geography.expl: The Pacific Ocean covers about 165.25 million sq km — larger than all land area combined. It contains the Mariana Trench.

geography.q: Which is the longest river in the world?
geography.expl: The Nile stretches approximately 6,650 km through northeastern Africa. The Amazon is the largest by water volume but slightly shorter.

geography.q: Which desert is the largest hot desert?
geography.expl: The Sahara covers about 9.2 million sq km across North Africa. Antarctica is the largest desert overall (cold desert).

geography.q: Which strait separates Europe from Africa?
geography.expl: The Strait of Gibraltar is only 14.3km at its narrowest, connecting the Atlantic to the Mediterranean.

geography.q: What is the capital of Australia?
geography.expl: Canberra was purpose-built as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne. It became the seat of government in 1927.

geography.q: What is the smallest country in the world?
geography.expl: Vatican City covers only 0.44 sq km and has about 800 residents. It became an independent state in 1929.

geography.q: What is the Ring of Fire?
opts: A volcanic zone around the Pacific
geography.expl: The Ring of Fire is a horseshoe-shaped zone where about 75% of the world's volcanoes and 90% of earthquakes occur.

geography.q: Which continent has the most countries?
geography.expl: Africa has 54 recognized countries. Asia has 48, Europe has 44-50, and South America has 12.

geography.q: What is the deepest point in the ocean?
geography.expl: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench reaches about 10,994m below sea level — deeper than Mount Everest is tall.

geography.q: What country is both in Europe and Asia?
geography.expl: Both Russia and Turkey span Europe and Asia. Russia's Ural Mountains divide the continents; Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus.

geography.q: What is the highest waterfall in the world?
geography.expl: Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 979m, named after aviator Jimmie Angel. Victoria Falls is the widest continuous curtain of water.

geography.q: What country has the most time zones?
geography.expl: France has 12 time zones due to overseas territories. Russia has 11 contiguous zones. The USA has 9 including territories.

geography.q: Which country has the most islands?
geography.expl: Sweden has approximately 267,570 islands, though only about 984 are inhabited. Indonesia has about 17,500 islands.

geography.q: Which African country was never colonized?
geography.expl: Ethiopia is one of only two African countries (along with Liberia) never colonized by a European power. It defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.

geography.q: What is the primary cause of Earth's seasons?
geography.expl: Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt means different hemispheres receive more direct sunlight at different times of the year. Distance from the sun has little effect.

math.q: What is the value of Pi to two decimal places?
math.expl: Pi (π) ≈ 3.14159... It's the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter and is an irrational number.

math.q: What is the square root of 144?
math.expl: 12 × 12 = 144. Perfect squares like 144 have integer square roots.
A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The smallest prime is 2 (the only even prime). Examples: 2,3,5,7,11...

math.q: What is the sum of angles in a triangle?
math.expl: The interior angles of any triangle in Euclidean geometry always sum to 180°. This was proven by Euclid around 300 BC.

opts: Each number is the sum of the two before
math.expl: The Fibonacci: 0,1,1,2,3,5,8,13,21... Each number is the sum of the two preceding ones. It appears throughout nature.
In a right triangle, a² + b² = c² where c is the hypotenuse. Example: 3² + 4² = 5² (9 + 16 = 25).

math.q: What is 2 to the power of 10?
math.expl: 2¹⁰ = 1024. This is why 1 kilobyte = 1024 bytes in computing. Powers of 2 are fundamental in computer science.

opts: A shape with all equal sides
A quadrilateral with opposite sides parallel
A triangle with two equal sides
A shape with four right angles
math.expl: A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal. Squares, rectangles, and rhombuses are special parallelograms.
5! = 5×4×3×2×1 = 120. Factorials grow extremely fast and are essential in combinatorics and probability.

math.q: What is the golden ratio approximately?
math.expl: The golden ratio (φ) ≈ 1.618. It appears in art, architecture, and nature — in spirals, proportions, and growth patterns.
Integration calculates the accumulated area under a curve. It's the reverse of differentiation. Together they form calculus.
e ≈ 2.71828... It's the base of natural logarithms. eˣ is its own derivative, making it central to calculus.

math.q: How many faces does a dodecahedron have?
math.expl: A regular dodecahedron has 12 pentagonal faces, 30 edges, and 20 vertices. It's one of the five Platonic solids.

math.q: What is the derivative of x³?
math.expl: Using the power rule: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹. So d/dx(x³) = 3x². The derivative gives the instantaneous rate of change.

opts: A word that reads the same forward and backward
language.expl: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Examples: 'racecar', 'madam', 'level'.

opts: A word that imitates a sound
language.expl: Onomatopoeia imitate sounds: 'buzz', 'hiss', 'bang', 'whisper'. Different languages often have different onomatopoeia for the same sounds.

opts: Words that sound the same but differ in meaning
language.expl: Homophones sound identical but have different meanings/spellings: 'to/too/two', 'their/there/they're', 'bare/bear'.

language.q: What is the most spoken language by native speakers?
language.expl: Mandarin Chinese has about 920 million native speakers. English has ~380 million native but ~1.5 billion total speakers.

language.q: Which language has the most words?
language.expl: English has an estimated 600,000+ words, largely due to borrowing from Latin, French, Germanic, and many other languages.

language.q: What is the origin of the word 'alphabet'?
language.expl: From the first two Greek letters: alpha (α) and beta (β). The Greek alphabet was adapted from Phoenician around 800 BC.

language.q: What is a semicolon used for?
opts: Creating a pause shorter than a period
language.expl: Semicolons connect two related independent clauses: 'It was getting late; we decided to leave.' They also separate items in complex lists.

language.q: What language family does English belong to?
language.expl: English is West Germanic, along with German and Dutch. Despite heavy French/Latin influence, its core grammar and basic vocabulary are Germanic.
Etymology traces word origins and meaning changes. E.g., 'nice' comes from Latin 'nescius' (ignorant), evolving through 'foolish' to 'pleasant'.

language.q: How many official languages does the UN have?
language.expl: The UN has 6 official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish, chosen for geographic representation.

language.q: How many letters are in the Japanese Hiragana syllabary?
language.expl: Hiragana has 46 basic characters, each representing a syllable. Japanese uses three writing systems: Hiragana, Katakana, and Kanji.
The subjunctive expresses wishes/demands/hypotheticals: 'If I were rich' (not 'was'), 'I suggest that he study' (not 'studies').
Linear A, used by the Minoan civilization (c. 1800-1450 BC), remains undeciphered. Linear B was decoded in 1952.

opts: A word that appears only once in a text or corpus
language.expl: It's a word that occurs only once within a context, either in the written record of an entire language, in the works of an author, or in a single text.

opts: Plants converting light to chemical energy
nature.expl: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. It's the primary source of Earth's oxygen.

nature.q: What is the fastest land animal?
nature.expl: Cheetahs reach 100-120 km/h in short bursts. Pronghorns sustain 88 km/h for much longer distances.
Symbiosis includes mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, one unaffected), and parasitism (one benefits, one harmed).
Hummingbirds can fly in any direction including backwards. Their wings rotate in a figure-8 pattern, beating up to 80 times/second.

opts: Variety of life in an ecosystem
nature.expl: Biodiversity includes species, genetic, and ecosystem diversity. The Amazon alone contains 10% of all known species.

nature.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
nature.expl: Octopuses have 3 hearts: one systemic heart for the body, two branchial hearts for the gills. They also have blue blood from copper-based hemocyanin.

nature.q: What layer of the Amazon rainforest receives the least sunlight?
nature.expl: The forest floor receives only 2-5% of sunlight. It's dark, humid, and covered in decomposing matter despite being the 'deepest' layer.

nature.q: What is the purpose of a flower's nectar?
nature.expl: Nectar attracts pollinators like bees and hummingbirds. In exchange, they transfer pollen between flowers, enabling fertilization.

nature.q: What is the tusk of a narwhal?
nature.expl: The narwhal tusk is an elongated left canine tooth with up to 10 million nerve endings, likely functioning as a sensory organ.

opts: Solar particles interacting with the atmosphere
nature.expl: Auroras occur when charged solar particles interact with Earth's magnetic field, exciting atmospheric gases. Green = oxygen at ~100km; red = oxygen higher; purple = nitrogen.

opts: A predator at the top of the food chain
A predator that only eats plants
nature.expl: Apex predators have no natural predators: lions, great whites, polar bears. They regulate prey populations and maintain ecosystem balance.

nature.q: What is the largest living organism on Earth?
nature.expl: A honey fungus in Oregon spans about 2,385 acres and is estimated at 2,400-8,650 years old. Blue whales are the largest animals.

nature.q: What animal can sleep for up to 3 years?
nature.expl: Some snail species can estivate for up to 3 years during drought, sealing their shells with mucus to retain moisture.
Chameleons have iridophores with nanocrystals. Adjusting crystal spacing reflects different wavelengths, changing apparent color.

nature.q: Which animal has the fastest punch in the animal kingdom?
nature.expl: The mantis shrimp can strike at 80 km/h (50 mph) underwater, generating a cavitation bubble that reaches temperatures nearly as hot as the surface of the sun.

culture.expl: Leonardo da Vinci painted it between 1503-1519. It hangs in the Louvre, Paris, protected by bulletproof glass.

culture.q: What is the Japanese art of paper folding called?
culture.expl: Origami: 'ori' (folding) + 'kami' (paper). Traditional origami uses a single square sheet with no cuts or glue.

culture.q: In which country did the Olympic Games originate?
culture.expl: Ancient Olympics began in 776 BC in Olympia, Greece. The modern Olympics were revived in 1896 in Athens.
A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black, spanning over 7 octaves. Bösendorfer makes a 97-key model.
Shakespeare wrote it around 1594-96, adapting from Arthur Brooke's 1562 poem. It's his most performed play.
Calligraphy means 'beautiful writing' from Greek. Major traditions include Chinese, Arabic, and Western calligraphy.

culture.q: What does red symbolize in Chinese culture?
culture.expl: Red symbolizes good fortune and prosperity in Chinese culture. It's used in weddings, Lunar New Year, and red envelopes (hongbao).
Diwali celebrates the victory of light over darkness. It lasts 5 days, featuring lamps (diyas), fireworks, rangoli art, and sweets.
Renaissance means 'rebirth' in French, referring to the revival of classical Greek and Roman culture beginning in 14th-century Italy.

culture.q: What is the Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos)?
opts: Mexican celebration honoring deceased loved ones
culture.expl: This Mexican holiday (Nov 1-2) celebrates deceased loved ones with ofrendas, marigolds, and sugar skulls, blending Aztec and Catholic traditions.
Legend says Emperor Shen Nung discovered tea in 2737 BC when leaves blew into his boiling water. China cultivated tea for millennia.

culture.q: What is the significance of the Torah?
opts: First five books of the Hebrew Bible
culture.expl: The Torah contains Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy — the foundation of Jewish law and tradition.
The haka is a ceremonial Maori war dance with rhythmic movements and chanting, performed at significant events including rugby matches.

opts: Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold
culture.expl: Kintsugi repairs broken pottery with lacquer mixed with gold, embracing imperfection — breakage becomes part of the object's beautiful history.

culture.q: What architectural style is the Sagrada Família?
culture.expl: Gaudí's Sagrada Família blends Art Nouveau with organic natural forms. Begun in 1882, it's still under construction.
